chief_complaint: sharp electric pain radiating down back of leg to ankle with numbness and positive straight leg raise after lifting heavy box
hpi_details: 38M warehouse worker presenting with acute onset of sharp, electric pain radiating from his low back down the posterior leg to the ankle, with associated numbness, since lifting a heavy box at work 3 days ago.
ideas: He thinks he severely pulled a deep muscle or slipped a bone out of place from lifting that heavy crate at work.
concerns: He is worried that the shooting nerve pain means permanent damage that will prevent him from lifting heavy boxes and doing warehouse work.
expectations: He hopes to receive a strong painkiller injection and an MRI scan to find out what popped in his lower back.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes conservative care (activity modification, NSAIDs, physical therapy) for 4-6 weeks before considering imaging or injection, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sharp electric pain radiating down back of leg to ankle with numbness and positive straight leg raise after lifting heavy box

Key HPI features: 38M warehouse worker presenting with acute onset of sharp, electric pain radiating from his low back down the posterior leg to the ankle, with associated numbness, since lifting a heavy box at work 3 days ago.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Antalgic gait, lumbar paraspinal tenderness and spasm, reduced lumbar flexion due to pain. Positive straight leg raise on the affected side reproducing radicular leg pain below the knee. Diminished ankle reflex (S1) and decreased sensation over the lateral foot/sole, with mildly reduced plantarflexion strength. No saddle anesthesia, normal rectal tone, no bowel/bladder dysfunction.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Lumbar spinal stenosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder incontinence).
management_principles: Screen thoroughly for cauda equina red flags (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder dysfunction, bilateral symptoms) at presentation and at every follow-up
First-line treatment is conservative: activity modification, NSAIDs, and structured physical therapy (e.g., McKenzie exercises), typically for 4-6 weeks before escalation
Reserve MRI for red-flag features, progressive or significant motor deficit, or failure to improve after 6 weeks of conservative care
Escalate to epidural steroid injection or surgical referral if conservative management fails or a significant motor deficit develops.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 38M warehouse worker presenting with acute onset of sharp, electric pain radiating from his low back down the posterior leg to the ankle, with associated numbness, since lifting a heavy box at work 3 days ago.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Antalgic gait, lumbar paraspinal tenderness and spasm, reduced lumbar flexion due to pain. Positive straight leg raise on the affected side reproducing radicular leg pain below the knee. Diminished ankle reflex (S1) and decreased sensation over the lateral foot/sole, with mildly reduced plantarflexion strength. No saddle anesthesia, normal rectal tone, no bowel/bladder dysfunction.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute L5/S1 lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica), most consistent with disc herniation, without cauda equina red flags.
reference_soap.plan: Begin conservative management: activity modification, NSAIDs, and a structured physical therapy program (e.g., McKenzie-directional exercises) with reassessment in 4-6 weeks. Reserve MRI for red-flag features, progressive neurologic deficit, or failure to improve after 6 weeks of conservative care. Refer for epidural steroid injection or surgical evaluation if conservative treatment fails or a significant motor deficit develops, and educate the patient on cauda equina warning signs requiring immediate return.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Lumbar Disc Herniation Radiculopathy Sciatica
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for sharp electric pain radiating down back of leg to ankle with numbness and positive straight leg raise after lifting heavy box
Determine when MRI imaging is warranted versus a trial of conservative therapy for acute sciatica
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: Compression or inflammation of a lumbar nerve root causing sharp radiating leg pain, numbness, and motor weakness.
red_flags: Cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder incontinence)

must_ask.say: Does the pain shoot down past your knee into your foot or toes?
Does coughing, sneezing, or sitting down make the leg pain much worse?
Have you noticed any numbness around your buttocks or loss of bowel or bladder control?
Does raising your straight leg while lying flat trigger the shooting pain?
Do you feel weakness when walking on your heels or toes?

history.answer: Three days ago, I lifted a heavy box at work and suddenly felt a sharp, shooting pain travel from my lower back all the way down the back of my right leg to my ankle.
The pain starts in my right lower back and shoots down the back of my thigh and calf, going past my knee down to my ankle.
It started suddenly three days ago while I was lifting a heavy crate off the ground at work.
It feels like a sharp, burning electric shock, and at its worst it gets up to a seven or eight out of ten.
Sitting down, bending forward, or coughing makes that electric pain shoot down my leg, while lying flat with my knees bent gives me a little relief.
No, the pain does not wake me up at night, and resting in bed actually feels much better than standing or sitting.
My back feels slightly tight for a couple of minutes when I first get out of bed, but it definitely does not last thirty minutes, and moving around does not make it better.
The outer side and bottom of my right foot feel numb and tingly, and pushing down on my toes feels slightly weak when I try to step.
No, I have normal bladder and bowel control, with no leakage or trouble peeing.
No, the sensation around my groin and private area feels completely normal.
Walking can trigger the pain if I take long strides, but bending forward or sitting down actually makes the pain worse rather than relieving it.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, night sweats, or unexpected weight loss.
No, I have never been diagnosed with cancer.
No recent infections, no spinal injections or acupuncture, and I have never used intravenous drugs.
No, I have never taken steroid medications, and I have never been told I have fragile bones.
No belly pain, no pulsating sensation in my abdomen, and no blood or pain when I urinate.
No red or painful eyes, no rash, no heel pain, and no loose stools.
I haven't taken any painkillers yet because I wanted to get evaluated by a doctor first.
I work full-time in a warehouse lifting and loading packages, and I am worried about being unable to do my job.
I thought I just pulled a deep back muscle or threw a bone out of place when I hoisted that heavy crate.
I'm really worried that I damaged a nerve permanently and won't be able to lift crates at the warehouse, which would cost me my job.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or kidney disease.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never stayed overnight in a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or vitamins.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco.
I drink a beer or two with friends once or twice a month, but nothing regular.
I live in an apartment with my wife, and she has been helping me with chores since my back started hurting.
My parents are both healthy in their sixties, and no one in my family has serious spine or joint diseases.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Antalgic gait favoring the right leg with a shortened stance phase; Romberg test is negative.
Tenderness and muscle spasm in the right lumbar paraspinal area, with a positive straight leg raise on the right at 40 degrees reproducing shooting leg pain below the knee.
Lumbar forward flexion is restricted by pain, while hip, knee, and ankle passive ranges of motion are full bilaterally.
Mild weakness in right ankle plantarflexion at 4/5 strength, with 5/5 strength in knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion, and great toe extension bilaterally.
Decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick over the lateral border of the right foot and sole, with normal sensation in the perianal area.
Diminished right Achilles tendon reflex (1+), while the left Achilles reflex and both patellar reflexes are normal (2+) with downgoing plantar responses.
Normal resting anal sphincter tone and normal voluntary contraction without tenderness or masses.
Soft, non-tender abdomen with no palpable masses or abnormal aortic pulsation.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion bilaterally.
